title: Counting Lattice Points in a Triangle
author: Math Beamer

frames.title: How many grid points fit?

body.text: Start with points $(x,y)$ whose coordinates are whole numbers.
Keep the points with $x+y\leq 4$, including the boundary.
Can you count them without checking every point?

frames.notes: Ask for a guess before revealing the last line.

frames.title: The grid for size four
frames.caption: The dots mark the grid points in the triangle.

frames.title: Count one row at a time

body.text: The bottom row has five points.
Move one row up and **lose one point** each time.

frames.title: Pair the long and short rows

body.bullet: The longest and shortest rows add up to six.
The next two rows add up to six as well.
The middle row has three points.

frames.title: The count for any size

body.text: Let $N(k)$ count whole-number pairs $(x,y)$ with $x+y\leq k$.
Pair the row lengths with the same list in reverse order.

frames.notes: Add the list of row lengths to its reversed copy and divide by two.

body.text: Send a grid point $(a,b)$ to the monomial $X^aY^b$.
The inequality $a+b\leq k$ bounds the **total degree**.
Let $N_d(k)$ count monomials of total degree at most $k$ in $d$ variables.
Introduce a slack exponent $a_{d+1}$ to reach degree $k$.
Place $d$ dividers among $k$ stars to count the solutions.
A triangle with legs of length $k$ has area $k^2/2$.
The leading term of the monomial count is **area**.
